concepts.title: Four Ds of Abnormality and Views of Abnormal Behaviour
concepts.section: Concepts of Abnormality and Psychological Disorders
concepts.definition: Psychological disorder is judged by four markers called the four Ds - deviance (extreme or unusual behaviour), distress (upsetting to self and others), dysfunction (blocking constructive daily activity) and danger; beyond these, one view equates abnormality with breaking social norms, while the better view labels behaviour abnormal when it is maladaptive, harming the well-being and growth of the person and group.
concepts.formula: four_ds = deviance + distress + dysfunction + danger ; maladaptive -> abnormal even if socially accepted
concepts.key_idea: Normality is not mere conformity: a conforming student who never asks questions out of fear can still be showing maladaptive behaviour; stigma keeps many people from seeking help.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy104.txt, Concepts of Abnormality (four Ds, norms-based vs maladaptive views, Activity 4.1, stigma discussion)
question_patterns: state the four Ds used to identify psychological disorder and explain each briefly

solution_steps.explain: a disorder tends to be deviant, distressing, dysfunctional and possibly dangerous - all four Ds point to failure of adaptation
behaviour is abnormal when it blocks optimal functioning and growth, so even conforming behaviour can qualify

worked_examples.q: Behaviour that blocks constructive daily activity shows which D of abnormality: dysfunction or deviance?

concepts.title: Historical Perspectives and Classification Systems
concepts.section: Historical Background / Classification of Psychological Disorders
concepts.definition: Explanations of disturbed behaviour have recurred as three perspectives - supernatural forces treated through exorcism or the shaman, the biological or organic approach locating trouble in body and brain, and the psychological approach blaming thought, feeling and perception; Galen extended Hippocrates' four humours much as Indian texts speak of vata, pitta and kapha. Today disorders are classified officially through the American Psychiatric Association's DSM-5 and the WHO's ICD-10, the scheme used in India.
concepts.formula: perspectives = supernatural + biological_organic + psychological ; manuals = dsm_5 (APA) + icd_10 (WHO)
concepts.key_idea: The reform movement and deinstitutionalisation grew from the eighteenth-century scientific attitude, and current thinking combines all three factors in the bio-psycho-social approach.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy104.txt, Historical Background (exorcism, four humours, witch-hunts, Weyer, Reform Movement) and Classification (DSM-5, ICD-10)
question_patterns: which three perspectives recur through the history of abnormal psychology?

solution_steps.explain: supernatural, biological or organic, and psychological explanations appear again and again from ancient Greece to the present
DSM-5 gives discrete clinical criteria per disorder while ICD-10, prepared by WHO, provides clinical features and diagnostic guidelines and serves officially in India

concepts.title: Models of Abnormal Behaviour and the Diathesis-Stress Model
concepts.definition: Each model spotlights different causes: the biological model ties disorders to neurotransmitter problems - low GABA with anxiety disorders, excess dopamine with schizophrenia, low serotonin with depression; the psychodynamic model reads symptoms as symbolic expressions of unconscious conflict from early childhood; the behavioural model treats disorder as maladaptive learning that can be unlearned; the cognitive model blames irrational assumptions and overgeneralisation; the humanistic-existential model cites blocked self-actualisation or avoided responsibility; and the socio-cultural model points to enmeshed families, labelling and social isolation. The diathesis-stress model joins them: a predisposition turns into disorder only when pathogenic stressors trigger it.
concepts.formula: gaba_low -> anxiety ; dopamine_excess -> schizophrenia ; serotonin_low -> depression ; disorder = diathesis (predisposition) triggered_by pathogenic_stressors
concepts.key_idea: No single gene causes a disorder; many genes plus stress combine, which is why the interactional bio-psycho-social view is widely accepted.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy104.txt, Factors Underlying Abnormal Behaviour (biological, psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic-existential, socio-cultural, diathesis-stress models)

an inherited biological aberration carries vulnerability; only exposure to pathogenic stressors converts the at-risk state into the actual disorder

concepts.title: Anxiety Disorders: Generalised, Panic, Phobias and Separation Anxiety
concepts.definition: Anxiety is a diffuse, vague, unpleasant feeling of fear and apprehension that becomes a disorder when it is intense enough to disturb effective functioning; its main forms are generalised anxiety disorder with objectless prolonged fear, hypervigilance and motor tension, panic disorder with recurrent surges of intense terror, phobias split into specific, social and agoraphobia, and separation anxiety disorder with developmentally inappropriate distress about leaving attachment figures.
concepts.key_idea: Normal examination nerves motivate, but a disorder brings rapid heart rate, breathlessness, sweating and sleeplessness that block everyday activity; Deb's driving-panic case shows panic growing into agoraphobic withdrawal.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy104.txt, Anxiety Disorders (Table 4.1, Deb's case, three phobia types, SAD in children)
question_patterns: at what stage does ordinary anxiety become an anxiety disorder? name its types

solution_steps.explain: anxiety counts as disordered when its level is high, distressing, and interfering with effective functioning rather than motivating
specific phobias target objects or situations, social phobia brings incapacitating fear before others, and agoraphobia is fear of unfamiliar situations that can trap people indoors

worked_examples.q: Objectless prolonged fear with hypervigilance marks which anxiety disorder: generalised or panic?

concepts.title: Obsessive-Compulsive and Trauma-Related Disorders
concepts.section: Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders / Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders
concepts.definition: In obsessive-compulsive disorder the person cannot stop thinking about an idea (obsession) or cannot resist repeating an act such as counting, checking or washing (compulsion); related conditions include hoarding, trichotillomania and excoriation. After disasters, blasts, accidents or war, survivors may develop post-traumatic stress disorder with recurrent dreams, flashbacks, impaired concentration and emotional numbing; adjustment disorder and acute stress disorder belong to the same trauma-related family.
concepts.formula: ocd = obsession (intrusive idea) + compulsion (repeated act) ; ptsd = flashbacks + nightmares + numbing after trauma
concepts.key_idea: Obsessions are unwanted and often shameful thoughts, while compulsions are rituals performed over and over; PTSD symptoms can surface long after the traumatic event ends.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy104.txt, Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders (hand-washing example), Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders (tsunami, bomb blasts, PTSD symptoms)

solution_steps.explain: the obsession is the inability to stop thinking about a particular idea, and the compulsion is the need to perform certain behaviours repeatedly
recurrent dreams, flashbacks, impaired concentration and emotional numbing follow extreme events such as earthquakes, accidents or war exposure

worked_examples.q: In OCD, the intrusive unwanted idea is the what: obsession or compulsion?

concepts.title: Somatic Symptom and Dissociative Disorders
concepts.section: Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders / Dissociative Disorders
concepts.definition: Somatic symptom and related disorders produce physical complaints without a biological cause: somatic symptom disorder centres on persistent body symptoms and frequent doctor visits, illness anxiety disorder on constant worry about developing a serious disease, and conversion disorders on sudden loss of body function such as paralysis, blindness or deafness after stress. Dissociative disorders sever the links between ideas and emotions: dissociative amnesia brings selective memory loss with no organic basis, dissociative fugue adds unexpected travel and a new identity, dissociative identity disorder shows alternate personalities, and depersonalisation or derealisation brings a dreamlike split from self and reality.
concepts.formula: somatic_group = somatic_symptom + illness_anxiety + conversion ; dissociative_group = amnesia + fugue + identity + depersonalisation
concepts.key_idea: Both families respond to stress, but somatic disorders express trouble through the body while dissociative disorders express it through memory, identity and the sense of reality.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy104.txt, Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders, Dissociative Disorders, Box 4.1 salient features

concepts.title: Depressive and Bipolar Disorders
concepts.section: Depressive Disorders / Bipolar and Related Disorders
concepts.definition: Major depressive disorder is a period of depressed mood or loss of interest and pleasure in most activities, joined by weight and sleep changes, tiredness, unclear thinking, agitation, worthlessness, guilt and thoughts of death; women face the highest risk in young adulthood, men in early middle age, and negative life events with weak social support add risk. Bipolar I disorder alternates mania with depression, sometimes punctuated by normal mood, and bipolar II and cyclothymic disorder are related forms.
concepts.formula: mdd = depressed_mood or loss_of_interest plus somatic_cognitive_symptoms ; bipolar = mania alternating with depression
concepts.key_idea: A previous suicidal attempt is the strongest risk factor for suicide, and suicidal thoughts turn into action only when they seem the only way out - suicides are preventable.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy104.txt, Depressive Disorders (risk factors: heredity, age, gender), Bipolar and Related Disorders, suicide risk factors and WHO measures

mania rarely stands alone; it usually alternates with depression, with stretches of normal mood possible in between

concepts.title: Schizophrenia: Positive, Negative and Psychomotor Symptoms
concepts.section: Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders
concepts.definition: Schizophrenia is a group of psychotic disorders in which personal, social and occupational functioning deteriorates through disturbed thought, strange perception, unusual emotion and motor abnormality. Positive symptoms are pathological excesses - delusions of persecution, reference, grandeur and control, disorganised speech with loosening of associations, neologisms and perseveration, hallucinations most often auditory, and inappropriate affect. Negative symptoms are pathological deficits - poverty of speech (alogia), blunted or flat affect, loss of volition (avolition) and social withdrawal. Psychomotor symptoms can reach catatonic stupor, rigidity or posturing.
concepts.key_idea: Shifting topics mid-speech is a positive symptom (formal thought disorder); hearing voices talking about the patient is a third-person auditory hallucination.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy104.txt, Symptoms of Schizophrenia (delusion types, thought disorder signs, hallucination senses, alogia, avolition, catatonia)

concepts.title: Neurodevelopmental Disorders and the Autism-Disability Link
concepts.definition: Neurodevelopmental disorders show up early, before or during early schooling, as deficits, excesses or delays in age-appropriate behaviour: ADHD combines inattention with hyperactivity-impulsivity; autism spectrum disorder brings widespread impairment in social interaction and communication plus stereotyped, restricted behaviour; intellectual disability means IQ near 70 or below with adaptive deficits before age 18; and specific learning disorder hampers reading, writing or mathematics despite normal instruction.
concepts.key_idea: About seventy of every hundred children on the autism spectrum also have intellectual disabilities; a child described as driven by a motor shows the hyperactive face of ADHD.

concepts.title: Eating Disorders and Substance-Related Disorders
concepts.section: Feeding and Eating Disorders / Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders
concepts.definition: Eating disorders revolve around food and body image: anorexia nervosa rests on a distorted body image that drives refusal to eat and compulsive exercise, bulimia nervosa alternates binges with purging through vomiting or laxatives, and binge eating brings frequent out-of-control eating past fullness. Substance-related and addictive disorders cover regular use of alcohol, heroin, cocaine and other substances that alter thinking, feeling and behaviour; repeated use builds tolerance and stopping brings withdrawal responses.
concepts.formula: eating_disorders = anorexia + bulimia + binge_eating ; dependence = tolerance + withdrawal
concepts.key_idea: Ethyl alcohol first depresses the brain areas governing judgment and inhibition, which is why drinkers feel overconfident before speech, memory and motor control fail.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy104.txt, Feeding and Eating Disorders, Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders, Box 4.2 effects of alcohol, Box 4.3 commonly abused substances

solution_steps.explain: anorexia starves through fear of being overweight, bulimia cancels binges with purging, and binge eating keeps out-of-control episodes without the purge
tolerance means the body needs greater amounts for the same effect, and withdrawal is the reaction that appears when intake stops
